segments.text: This woman has fourteen days to prove to her soon-to-be ex-husband that she can give their daughter a home. If she can't, she says, things will get ugly. Her daughter Hollis corrects her: uglier.
So Bram tours a huge Manhattan brownstone. Four floors, an elevator, and a past owner who was a paranoid recluse worth around thirty million dollars, half of which nobody can find.

Then she notices a corner of the bedroom that looks off. It's a panic room, which the agent calls a castle keep: steel walls, a buried phone line of its own, its own air, and monitors that watch almost every corner of the house.

Bram, who hates small spaces, asks the agent if he's ever read any Poe. He thinks she means a singer. And the steel door has a sensor that won't let it close on anything blocking it. Keep that in mind.
On their first night, they eat pizza on the floor. When the ex-husband comes up, the kid says what her mom is thinking, and Bram's whole parenting strategy is: I agree, but don't.
That night, three burglars bypass the alarm and find out the house isn't empty. Thanks to a fourteen-business-day escrow mix-up, a woman and a little girl are already asleep upstairs.

Lena wants out on the spot: not with people. The planner, Rufus, swears it will only take forty-five minutes, a number he'll repeat all night. Then Lena realizes the third guy, Milo, is a stranger with a gun. Where did you get this clown, he asks.
Rufus calls himself a third-generation idiot who finally had one good idea, and plays his trump card: fourteen million dollars upstairs, enough to get Lena out of the hole for good. Lena stays.

Upstairs, Bram spots them on the monitors, wakes Hollis, and the two race the burglars to the panic room, slamming the door just in time. Then comes the bad news: Bram never hooked up the room's phone.
Inside, she quietly asks Hollis if she feels shaky or cold.
Bram bluffs that the police are coming. The men answer with a sign: what we want is in that room. Coached by her own daughter, Bram finally swears at them: get out of my house.
Here's the irony: Lena spent ten years building rooms like this to keep people out, and now has to figure out how to get in. You can't break in, he says. You make them come out.
In the cramped room, Bram starts to panic. Hollis distracts her with a chicken joke, and when Bram breaks down, it's the kid who screams at her to stay present.
Then gas starts pouring into the vents. Lena yells that they're trying to scare them, not kill them, and points out they can't get into the room if the two pass out. Rufus's answer: oh.

Hollis knows how to signal S.O.S., which she learned from Titanic. They flash it at a neighbor, who doesn't care. Downstairs, an argument over shares reveals Rufus meant to split the money only two ways, until Lena asks if he took a nap in math class.
It turns out it's Rufus's own grandfather they're robbing. And Milo, who talks like a movie gangster, is actually a bus driver from Flatbush.
Bram decides to risk it. If I can't get back, she tells Hollis, just close the door. She dashes to her bedroom, grabs her cell phone and dives back in, and there's no signal inside.

So she splices into the main phone line, which Rufus forgot to cut, and reaches 911, who put her on hold. Then a garbled call reaches Hollis's father. Bram swears he'll come because they're still a family.
Then Hollis confesses that she's dizzy and thirsty. She's diabetic, her sugar is dropping fast, and her Glucagon shot is in the little fridge in her bedroom, outside the room.

Rufus gives up. He'll make an anonymous tip and inherit the money legally, and he offers the others five hundred bucks for their time. Milo says nobody leaves, and when Rufus heads for the door, Milo turns on him. Who's the clown now? Then he gives Lena to the count of three to find a way in.

Hollis's father arrives and is captured. They beat him on camera to make Bram open up, and he shouts at her not to open the door no matter what. Even Lena begs Milo to stop because the kid is watching. And Hollis whispers: you gotta jab me, Mommy.
When the dust settles, the burglars are inside the panic room with Hollis, and Bram is outside, screaming that her daughter needs her medicine.

Lena asks what happens without the shot. Coma. Die. So he gives it to her himself, talking her through it while confessing six straight years of bad cards: his house, his car, his wife. Milo's response: congratulations, you saved her life for ten minutes.
Then two police officers knock. One even offers Bram a way to secretly signal for help. Knowing her daughter is a hostage, she sends them away with a mortifying story about a drunken call to her ex.
The safe opens, and Milo lays out the plan: the kid now, the other two after. Lena refuses.
The finale is pure chaos: a wall from the neighbor's house, screaming hostages, and Bram with Milo's gun. Lena grabs the money and runs, right into the police, who tell him to put his hands up.
Later, Bram and Hollis are back to house hunting, debating uptown near Dad or somewhere cooler. Wherever they end up, it probably won't have a panic room.
